Reproductive output in the Razorbelly scad (Alepes kleinii) has been characterized through examination of gravid females captured in coastal waters of the southeastern Arabian Sea. At a water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], a single mature female measuring 16.9 cm in total length was found to produce a batch of approximately 35,131 eggs [N_R_i = a batch of approximately 35,131 eggs] during a single spawning event. The species exhibits a reproductively active period during which an individual female typically completes two spawning events each season [F_R_i = two spawning events each season]. The high batch fecundity, which is consistent with values reported for other small planktivorous carangids, yields a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 193 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 193 eggs per day]. The yolk-sac larva that emerges from the pelagic, transparent egg weighs only 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams] at the moment of eclosion, reflecting the minimal maternal investment allocated per offspring. This tiny neonate, measuring less than three millimeters in length at hatching, depends entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves for the first several days of life, a critical period during which the mouth remains unopened and swimming capacity is rudimentary.

The transition to exogenous feeding marks a pivotal phase in the early life history of Alepes kleinii, occurring once the yolk reserves are nearly exhausted. Under the thermal regime of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C] typical of the species' tropical inshore nursery grounds, hatchlings require approximately six days [ab = approximately six days] to complete yolk-sac resorption and reach the point where first prey capture becomes possible. This brief lecithotrophic stage places a premium on the timely availability of suitable planktonic prey, as larvae that fail to initiate feeding within a narrow window after yolk depletion face starvation. The newly feeding larva, now an actively swimming member of the ichthyoplankton community, experiences rapid allometric growth during the ensuing weeks as it progresses through the preflexion and flexion stages before ultimately reaching the postflexion stage and initiating metamorphosis. The high fecundity exhibited by the species is consistent with an r-selected reproductive strategy that offsets heavy early-life mortality through the production of numerous, small offspring.

As juvenile Razorbelly scad grow and approach sexual maturation, a distinct inflection point in the length-weight relationship becomes apparent. Females attain puberty at a total length of 12.9 cm [Lp = 12.9 cm], a size that corresponds to a wet weight of 23 grams [Wwp = 23 grams] based on the allometric scaling relationship documented for this carangid species. This transition from the juvenile to the reproductively viable state is marked by the onset of gonadal recrudescence, during which oocytes begin vitellogenesis and spermatocytes initiate their maturation cycle. The size at first reproduction is considerably smaller than the ultimate length achieved by fully grown individuals, indicating that the species continues to allocate substantial resources to somatic growth even after achieving reproductive competence. Comparative data from congeneric species within the Carangidae suggest that the length at which 50% of individuals are mature corresponds closely to the 12.9 cm [Lp = 12.9 cm] threshold documented for Alepes kleinii in this population.

The maximum body size recorded for Alepes kleinii indicates that individuals can reach an ultimate total length of 18.2 cm [Li = 18.2 cm], with the largest confirmed specimens corresponding to a predicted ultimate wet weight of 64.6 grams [Wwi = 64.6 grams] as derived from the allometric scaling relationship. This asymptotic size is modest in comparison to many carangid predators, reflecting the species' ecological role as a small, schooling planktivore that forages in the coastal pelagic zone. Field surveys of age structure suggest that the species attains its maximum body dimensions relatively quickly, with growth rates decelerating markedly after the onset of reproductive maturity. The length-weight relationship used to estimate adult mass has been validated against direct measurements from freshly captured individuals spanning the full size range, confirming that the exponent of 3.0 provides an excellent fit to the empirical data. Sexual dimorphism in final body size appears minimal, with both males and females achieving comparable asymptotic dimensions under similar environmental conditions.

Longevity records for the Razorbelly scad in the wild, based on otolith increment analysis and mark-recapture studies conducted at the prevailing water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately five years [am = approximately five years]. This relatively short life history is characteristic of small, fast-growing tropical teleosts that face intense predation pressure throughout ontogeny. The oldest individuals encountered in population surveys typically show signs of reproductive senescence, with reduced fecundity and lower condition factors compared to younger, prime-age spawners. Compared to other carangids of similar body size, such as certain species of the genus Decapterus that may persist for up to eight years in cooler waters, the five-year lifespan of Alepes kleinii reflects the accelerated life-history pace imposed by its warm tropical habitat. The combination of early maturation, high batch fecundity, and a moderately extended spawning season allows Alepes kleinii to maintain stable population numbers despite the substantial losses suffered during the vulnerable early larval stages.
